strengths: Rigorous theoretical contribution: the paper formalizes four physically motivated axioms (locality, permutation equivariance, orientation covariance, energy balance/passivity) and proves a local Jacobian-level reduction theorem showing that under these axioms, mesh dynamics must factor into a port-Hamiltonian form with a topology-fixed, signed-incidence conservative interconnection and separately learnable metric/dissipation operators. The full proof (Appendix A) is careful and the argument for why each axiom is necessary (via counterexamples/relaxations) is a nice touch.

The electromagnetism worked example (Appendix B) nicely illustrates that Maxwell's equations and topological invariants (discrete div B=0, charge-free div D=0) emerge as consequences of the theorem rather than being assumed, lending credibility to the abstract framework.

Extensive and carefully designed empirical validation: analytic plane-wave benchmarks (grid and Delaunay meshes), a dissipative/Rayleigh-damped variant, a multi-faceted physics-consistency battery (wave speed, canonical consistency, PDE residual, equipartition, momentum, vector-field alignment, amplitude/phase), three types of OOD generalization (frequency, resolution, parameter shift), a real dataset from The Well (acoustic scattering), a nonlinear state-dependent toy problem, a targeted ablation study isolating which axioms matter, and a computational cost analysis.

MeshFT-Net achieves consistently strong results across nearly all these settings, often by orders of magnitude in energy drift and physical-consistency diagnostics, while using dramatically fewer parameters (642 vs ~100k-200k) and lower latency/memory than baselines, supporting the practical value of the inductive bias.

The ablation study (Table 9) is a valuable sanity check that directly interrogates the theorem's necessity claims (breaking orientation, topology, metric positivity, or learning J directly) and shows measurable degradation consistent with the theory.
weaknesses: The empirical scope is narrow relative to the motivating applications (fluid/solid mesh simulation à la MeshGraphNets): most experiments are on linear 2D plane-wave/wave-equation settings on regular or Delaunay meshes; the single nonlinear/state-dependent experiment is a small synthetic "shallow-water-style" toy problem rather than a realistic nonlinear PDE, so the paper does not convincingly demonstrate the approach on the complex, nonlinear, large-deformation problems that originally motivated learned mesh simulators.

The real-data validation (acoustic scattering from The Well) is comparatively thin: it presents only qualitative pressure-field snapshots (Fig. 3) without a quantitative table comparing MeshFT-Net against the same baselines used elsewhere (MGN, HNN, etc.), making it hard to assess relative real-world performance.

The main experiments adopt the state-independent, quadratic-storage simplification (Corollary 3.4) almost throughout, while the more general nonlinear/state-dependent formulation (Section 4 "General" case) is essentially only lightly touched by the small toy ablation in 5.5; this leaves a gap between the generality claimed by the theorem and what is actually validated.

Some baselines (e.g., PI-MGN) diverge (">100") in many OOD and physics-consistency conditions, which raises a question about whether baselines were adequately tuned/matched in capacity or training budget for a fully fair comparison, especially since MeshFT-Net uses orders of magnitude fewer parameters and a specialized symplectic integrator that baselines do not share architecturally.

The paper does not include a direct empirical comparison to the closely related data-driven exterior calculus approach (Trask et al., 2022), despite discussing it at length in related work, which would have been a natural and informative baseline given the topology-metric split shared by both methods.

The treatment of boundaries, external sources, and non-mesh-conforming heterogeneities is only briefly mentioned (e.g., sponge layers for open boundaries in the acoustic scattering experiment) without deeper theoretical or empirical exploration, leaving open how well the framework handles more complex boundary/source conditions common in real applications.

The manuscript is dense and notation-heavy (many appendices with lemmas/corollaries), which, combined with reliance on promised (not yet reviewed) supplementary code, makes full independent reproducibility somewhat harder to verify at this stage.

strengths: A genuine theoretical contribution: rather than positing a port-Hamiltonian template, the paper derives (Theorem 3.3, with a careful multi-lemma proof in Appendix B) that locality, permutation equivariance, orientation covariance, and an energy-balance/passivity condition together force the Jacobian of any admissible mesh dynamics to factor into a topology-fixed skew-symmetric incidence wiring plus a metric/dissipation part. This gives a principled, falsifiable rationale for the common DEC-style topology/metric split rather than assuming it outright.

Very extensive empirical program: analytic plane-wave tests on regular and Delaunay meshes, a dissipative benchmark, five/six physics-consistency diagnostics (wave speed, canonical consistency, PDE residual, equipartition, momentum, vector-field alignment), OOD shifts in frequency/resolution/wave-speed, a real dataset (The Well acoustic scattering), nonlinear/heterogeneous lattice and elasticity benchmarks, and multiple targeted ablations (topology-vs-metric separation, state-dependent coupling, and principle-level ablations that individually break orientation, topology, or metric positivity) that directly test the necessity of each theorem assumption.

Strong and fairly matched baseline suite (MGN, MGN-HP, HNN, PI-MGN, FNO, GraphCON) trained under identical protocols/integrators, which strengthens the comparative claims beyond a simple straw-man MGN comparison.

Reports computational cost (latency, memory, parameter count) showing large efficiency gains, and provides an EM-theory worked example (Appendix C) that grounds the abstract theorem in a concrete, checkable physical system (Maxwell's equations) with explicit topological invariants preserved.

Honest scoping of claims: the paper explicitly states the reduction is local/Jacobian-level and does not claim a single global port-Hamiltonian representation, and the appendix ablations test sharpness of each assumption rather than merely asserting it.
weaknesses: Nearly all quantitative benchmarks are synthetic problems (linear/near-linear wave equations, lattice oscillators) whose data-generating processes are essentially expressible within the exact DEC/port-Hamiltonian template the model imposes; this risks the strong numerical superiority being partly an artifact of matching the inductive bias to the data-generating structure rather than evidence of broader applicability to physics that is not naturally expressible this way (e.g., strongly nonlocal, advection-dominated, or turbulent phenomena).

The one real-world dataset (The Well acoustic scattering, Sec. 5.4) is evaluated only qualitatively (visual snapshots) with no quantitative table comparing MeshFT-Net against the baselines used elsewhere in the paper, leaving the central 'transfer to realistic data' claim less substantiated than the synthetic results.

Completeness of the local, permutation-equivariant linear basis in Lemma B.1 (restricted to {Id, A_k, D_{k-1}, D_k^T}) is asserted rather than rigorously justified via a representation-theoretic or exhaustive argument; a reader cannot easily verify that no other local, equivariant linear operators exist on general oriented complexes.

Experimental scale remains modest (grids up to 128×128, meshes with hundreds to a few thousand nodes), so scalability and behavior on large, high-resolution, or 3D meshes relevant to realistic engineering/scientific simulation remain unverified.
The abstract states 'the code is available at' with no actual link provided in the manuscript, undermining verifiable reproducibility at submission time.

Many reported metrics (e.g., Table 2, 4) lack variance/uncertainty estimates in the main text (only some appendix tables include std), making it harder to judge the significance of certain smaller gaps between MeshFT-Net and the strongest baselines (e.g., HNN in some columns).

strengths: The paper provides a rigorous, principle-driven derivation (Theorem 3.3 and its proof in Appendix B) showing that locality, permutation equivariance, orientation covariance, and an energy-balance/passivity condition together force a local port-Hamiltonian factorization with signed-incidence conservative wiring. This is a genuine theoretical contribution that goes beyond simply postulating a PH template, as is common in prior structure-preserving learning work (HNN, GFINNs, port-Hamiltonian NNs).

The resulting architecture (MeshFT-Net) is simple, lightweight (only ~642 parameters vs. 100k-200k for baselines), and computationally efficient (Table 15), while achieving substantially better energy conservation, dispersion accuracy, and long-horizon stability than MGN, MGN-HP, HNN, FNO, GraphCON, and PI-MGN across a wide range of settings.

The empirical evaluation is unusually extensive for a methods paper: analytic plane-wave benchmarks (regular/Delaunay meshes), a dissipative benchmark, detailed physics-consistency diagnostics (wave speed, canonical consistency, PDE residual, equipartition, momentum), OOD generalization under frequency/resolution/parameter shifts, real acoustic-scattering data from The Well, nonlinear/heterogeneous lattice and elasticity benchmarks, and multiple targeted ablations (topology-vs-metric separation, orientation removal, topology scrambling, indefinite metric, learned-J variants, state-dependent coupling).

The connection to discrete exterior calculus and electromagnetism (Appendix C) is a nice concrete illustration that grounds the abstract theorem in a familiar physical system (Maxwell's equations) and clarifies why the topology-fixed interconnection eliminates spurious modes (e.g., discrete divergence-free constraints).

The ablation studies (Table 14, Table 7, Table 8) directly and convincingly isolate the causal role of each assumption (orientation, topology, metric positivity), which strengthens the causal story linking the theorem to the empirical benefits observed.
weaknesses: The bulk of the quantitative comparisons rely on synthetic, mostly linear-wave data (analytic plane waves on periodic 2D grids/Delaunay meshes) generated by the authors themselves; the single real-world dataset (acoustic scattering from The Well) is evaluated mostly qualitatively (Fig. 3, visual snapshots) without a quantitative table comparing MeshFT-Net against baselines on this dataset, which weakens the claim of realistic applicability.

The practical instantiation used throughout most experiments assumes a quadratic, state-independent storage function Gθ (Section 4, 'Quadratic first-order model'), which effectively restricts the learned dynamics to linear wave/elastodynamics-type systems; while some nonlinear lattice benchmarks are included, they are lower-dimensional toy systems (1D/2D lattices) rather than full continuum nonlinear PDEs, so the practical scope is considerably narrower than the general nonlinear PH claims in Section 3 and the abstract.

Baseline configurations (MGN, MGN-HP, HNN, PI-MGN) appear to use fairly small, homogeneous architectures (4 layers, width 64) without evidence of extensive hyperparameter tuning; some baselines diverge or perform extremely poorly in several tables (e.g., PI-MGN >100 in nearly every OOD column, MGN/MGN-HP blowing up by orders of magnitude even in in-distribution energy drift), which raises concerns about whether these comparisons are fully fair or whether the baselines are under-tuned/mis-specified for the task.

Several central tables (e.g., Tables 2-8) report only means over 3-5 seeds without variance or significance testing, and differences of many orders of magnitude are treated as self-evidently meaningful without statistical characterization of noise, which can overstate the robustness of the comparisons.

The theoretical novelty relative to closely related prior work (data-driven exterior calculus with fixed incidence operators and learned Hodge stars, Trask et al. 2022; DEC-based structure preservation) is somewhat incremental — the main claimed advance is deriving the topology/metric split from physical axioms rather than assuming it, but the resulting practical parameterization (fix D_k, learn SPD/PSD metric and dissipation blocks) is essentially the same recipe used in that prior line of work.

The Impact Statement is entirely boilerplate and provides no substantive discussion of limitations, potential misuse, or failure modes of the approach, despite the paper explicitly acknowledging (in the ablations) that violating any of the four assumptions can lead to severe instability -- a discussion of when the modeling assumptions (e.g., state-independent metric, fixed mesh topology, no topology change over time) might fail for real physical systems (e.g., fracture, topology change, contact) is largely missing from the main text.

strengths: The central theoretical contribution—Theorem 3.3—is a genuine reduction result rather than a posited template: starting from four physically motivated axioms (locality, permutation equivariance, orientation covariance, energy balance/passivity), the paper derives (with a full, carefully structured proof in Appendix B) that admissible dynamics must locally factor into a port-Hamiltonian form with a topology-fixed, signed-incidence conservative interconnection. This clarifies precisely what must be hard-coded vs learned, which is a conceptually clean and useful insight beyond prior 'assume a PH/GENERIC template and fit it' approaches.

The electromagnetism worked example (Appendix C) is a nice sanity check, showing the framework recovers source-free Maxwell's equations and automatically yields divergence-free/charge-free invariants as a structural byproduct rather than a soft penalty.

Extensive and varied empirical validation: analytic plane-wave benchmarks (grid and Delaunay), dissipative/Rayleigh-damped settings, model-agnostic physics-consistency diagnostics (dispersion, canonical consistency, PDE residual, equipartition, momentum), OOD shifts (frequency/resolution/wave-speed), real data from The Well (acoustic scattering with discontinuous media), nonlinear/heterogeneous elasticity, and several nonlinear lattice systems (FPU, damped phi^4, sine-Gordon, state-dependent coupling).

Strong, consistent baseline comparisons (MGN, MGN-HP, HNN, PI-MGN, FNO, GraphCON) show large, often orders-of-magnitude improvements in energy drift, momentum conservation, and long-horizon stability, while also being far more parameter- and compute-efficient (Table 15).

Careful and well-targeted ablations: the topology-vs-metric separation ablation (Sec 5.6/Appendix D.8) and the principle-level ablations (Appendix D.9, e.g., No-Orientation, Scrambled-Topology, Indefinite-Metric, Learned-J variants) directly test the necessity of each theorem assumption and support the causal story rather than just correlational performance gains.
Reasonable reproducibility effort: detailed hyperparameters, data-generation procedures, and code availability are provided throughout the appendix.
weaknesses: The reduction theorem is explicitly a pointwise/Jacobian-level local statement (acknowledged by the authors), and the practical instantiation used in essentially all experiments is the further-restricted quadratic, state-independent-metric case (Sec. 4). The fully general nonlinear-storage-function instantiation described in Sec. 4 ('General' case with convex Hθ and dissipation potential Ψθ) is never actually evaluated, so the paper's empirical support covers a narrower slice of the theory than is presented.

Most core experiments (analytic plane-wave, physics-consistency, OOD, Well acoustic scattering) are 2D linear/near-linear wave-type problems. While Appendix D.6 adds nonlinear lattice and heterogeneous-elasticity tests, the paper does not evaluate on the fluid/turbulence-type problems (e.g., Navier–Stokes, complex deformable-body contact) where MeshGraphNets-style methods are most commonly deployed and where the topology–metric separation would be a stronger differentiator; this leaves open how the approach scales to harder, more irreversible/turbulent regimes.

The proof's local symmetry basis (Lemma B.1) presupposes that admissible local, permutation-equivariant linear maps are spanned by exactly {Id, adjacency, boundary, coboundary}; while defensible for linear neighborhood aggregation, this is itself a structural assumption about the function class (not purely a consequence of L/P) that somewhat pre-determines the incidence-wiring conclusion, and this restriction could be discussed more explicitly as a modeling choice rather than purely a 'deduced' fact.

The paper does not compare against some of the stronger structure-preserving baselines it discusses in related work (e.g., bracket-based GNNs of Gruber et al. 2023, GFINNs/GENERIC models, data-driven exterior calculus of Trask et al. 2022), which would be more informative comparators than MGN/HNN variants for validating the topology–metric separation claim specifically.

Reporting conventions such as capping diverged baseline values at '>100' obscure the true magnitude of divergence and make some comparisons less precise/interpretable than fully reported numbers would be.

The Rayleigh-type dissipation model used throughout is fairly simple; it is unclear how well the framework extends to more complex, history-dependent, or plastic/irreversible dissipative processes beyond linear damping.
